title: Calibration evidence
purpose: Inspect the recorded instrument model, compare temporary calibration fits, and trace the result revisions that use this evidence.
summary: Inspect recorded calibration evidence and linked result revisions. Calculate a linear or quadratic fit or the average calibration factor. Compare standards’ back-calculated errors with limits from your method or SOP.

tasks.title: Check the curve’s source and points
steps: Compare the model, units and source with the laboratory’s instrument record.

tasks.title: Fit a linear or quadratic model
steps: In [[Calibration fit worksheet]], choose [[Model]] and [[Weighting]]. For [[Linear through origin]], leave [[Weighting]] blank or choose [[Unweighted (equal weights)]].
To compare errors, enter a [[Maximum absolute percent error]]. If your method uses a different limit at the lowest concentration, also enter [[Maximum error at lowest concentration]].
Select [[Calculate fit]]. Review the [[Equation]], fitted coefficients and statistics.
In [[Standard points]], review [[Absolute percent error]] and, if you entered limits, [[Limit comparison]].

tasks.title: Inspect the average calibration factor
steps: Choose [[Average calibration factor]] under [[Model]]. Leave [[Weighting]] blank or choose [[Unweighted (equal weights)]].
Select [[Calculate fit]] and review the [[Mean calibration factor]], [[Sample standard deviation]] and [[Relative standard deviation (RSD)]].
Check [[Relative standard error (RSE)]] for the overall fit to the recorded concentrations.
In [[Standard points]], check the factors, predicted responses, residuals, [[Back-calculated concentration]] and [[Absolute percent error]].

tasks.title: Inspect a result that uses this curve
steps: In [[Result revisions using this calibration]], select a sample ID.
Read that revision’s calibration and verification snapshot beside its result.

tasks.title: Record a correction
steps: Return to the batch and select [[Record calibration]] to create a distinct record.
Enter a new revision of the affected result with the intended evidence and reason.

good_to_know: This record is immutable. Recording another curve does not change any existing result or issued report.
Follow your method and laboratory SOP for model selection and acceptance. [[Linear through origin]], [[Average calibration factor]] and inverse weighting need all concentrations to be positive.
In [[Quadratic]], a turning or constant curve blocks back-calculation. A response outside the fitted response range blocks it for that point.
A selected verification correction holds submission, approval and release until a new result revision records current evidence.
The people who recorded a selected curve or verification cannot review or release its result.

sections.title: Access and identity
paragraphs: Active staff with an application role can read this page; clients cannot. The header identifies the analytical batch, frozen analyte, method code/version and matrix. The batch link opens the run. Recorded evidence is a record state, not a scientific acceptance decision.

items.label: Calibration reference
items.description: The immutable instrument/run identifier within its batch.

items.label: Calibration time
items.description: The recorded actual calibration event, displayed in laboratory local time with zone.

items.label: Instrument-reported model
items.description: The supplied equation, fit and weighting description stored as instrument evidence.

items.label: Concentration unit / Response unit
items.description: The frozen units for the standard concentrations and instrument responses; no conversion occurs.

items.label: Source reference
items.description: The instrument output or laboratory source that the recorder supplied. The application does not retain an original instrument file here.

items.label: Equipment at recording
items.description: Equipment identity recorded on the batch when the curve was saved, or Not recorded. Later equipment edits do not rewrite this fact.

items.label: Recorded by / Recorded at
items.description: The staff account and time that created this evidence.

sections.title: Calibration fit worksheet
paragraphs: Staff who can read the calibration can use the worksheet. Linear and quadratic fits use least squares with a free intercept. Linear through origin fits the slope by least squares with the intercept fixed at zero. Average calibration factor takes the arithmetic mean of observed response divided by concentration for concentration-based external standards. Every model uses each recorded row in the frozen units, including replicates.

A quadratic fit needs at least three distinct concentrations. Each other model needs at least two. Linear through origin, average calibration factor and either inverse weighting require every concentration to be positive. Linear through origin rejects a recorded zero-concentration standard and adds no observation at zero.

An explicitly empty or unrecognized model, an incompatible weighting or an invalid limit shows a field error and keeps your entries. When the model cannot use the recorded points, Fit unavailable explains why. The recorded points remain visible in both cases.

Calculated values display up to 12 significant digits. Predicted responses, residuals, back-calculated concentrations and percent errors use the unrounded coefficients or mean factor. Fits and limits are temporary worksheet comparisons. Links from result revisions refer to the frozen instrument evidence. Use the laboratory’s procedure and configured QC checks for method acceptance.

items.label: Model
items.description: Choose Linear for a straight line with a fitted intercept, Linear through origin for a straight line with a fixed zero intercept, Quadratic for a second-degree polynomial or Average calibration factor to average the standard factors. Linear is selected when you first open the worksheet and when you follow a worksheet link that specifies only a weighting.

items.label: Weighting
items.description: Unweighted (equal weights) gives every row the same weight. Linear and quadratic fits require a selection and also support 1/x (inverse concentration) and 1/x² (inverse concentration squared). For Linear through origin and Average calibration factor, leave Weighting blank or choose Unweighted (equal weights).

items.label: Maximum absolute percent error
items.description: Optional general limit, in percent, supplied by the laboratory. A blank limit leaves the comparison columns hidden. Zero is valid. Each limit must be a finite, nonnegative number with at most 14 whole digits, 10 decimal places and 60 input characters.

items.label: Maximum error at lowest concentration
items.description: Optional limit, in percent, that overrides the general maximum for every point tied at the lowest recorded concentration, including replicates and a recorded zero. This field requires a general maximum. A blank override applies the general maximum to every point.

items.label: Calculate fit
items.description: Calculate using the selected model and weighting. A successful fit appears alongside the recorded evidence, with a comparison for each standard when you give a maximum. Change a selection or limit and calculate again to compare results.

items.label: Equation
items.description: Linear shows y = slope × x + intercept. Linear through origin shows y = slope × x. Quadratic shows y = a × x² + b × x + intercept. Average calibration factor shows y = mean factor × x. Here x is the recorded concentration and y is the predicted instrument response.

items.label: Mean calibration factor
items.description: The arithmetic mean of the calibration factors, in response units per concentration unit. Every recorded point contributes equally, including replicates.

items.label: Sample standard deviation
items.description: The spread of the individual standard factors in response units per concentration unit. The worksheet uses the number of points minus one as the divisor in the variance calculation.

items.label: Relative standard deviation (RSD)
items.description: Sample standard deviation divided by the mean factor and multiplied by 100. For a positive mean this equals the RSE because each relative concentration error equals its factor’s deviation from the mean divided by the mean. The worksheet shows an explanation when the mean is zero or negative.

items.label: Pearson correlation coefficient (r)
items.description: A unitless measure of the strength and direction of the linear relationship between concentration and observed response. It appears only for Linear with Unweighted (equal weights). The coefficient ranges from −1 to +1 and has the same sign as the fitted slope. Each recorded point, including replicates, counts separately. Identical observed responses leave r undefined. With varying responses, zero means there is no linear correlation. The worksheet calculates r from the unrounded fit. Apply your method and laboratory SOP for acceptance.

items.label: Coefficient of determination (R²)
items.description: A unitless measure shown after a successful Linear or Quadratic fit. It is one minus the sum of weighted squared response residuals divided by the sum of weighted squared deviations of the observed responses from their weighted mean. The calculation uses the selected weights and unrounded fit, with each recorded point, including replicates, counted separately. Identical observed responses leave R² unavailable because there is no response variation. A displayed zero means the fit explains none of the response variation. Use R² to inspect the fit and apply your method and laboratory SOP for acceptance.

items.label: Relative standard error (RSE)
items.description: Available for Linear and Average calibration factor. For each recorded point, subtract the recorded concentration from its unrounded back-calculated concentration and divide by the recorded concentration. Square these relative errors, sum them, divide by the degrees of freedom, take the square root and multiply by 100. Replicates count separately. Weighting applies to fitting the line. RSE is unavailable when any recorded concentration, the fitted slope or the mean factor is zero, or when there are too few points. A negative slope or factor still allows RSE.

items.label: RSE degrees of freedom
items.description: The number of recorded points minus the number of fitted terms. Linear uses two terms (slope and intercept), and Average calibration factor uses one (the mean factor). RSE requires a positive difference.

items.label: Slope / Linear coefficient (b)
items.description: The coefficient of concentration, expressed in response units per concentration unit. For a straight line, it gives the change in response per unit of concentration everywhere.

items.label: Quadratic coefficient (a)
items.description: The coefficient of concentration squared, expressed in response units per squared concentration unit. It describes the curvature and appears only for a quadratic fit.

items.label: Intercept
items.description: The response at zero concentration, in response units. Linear and quadratic fit this coefficient. Linear through origin fixes it at zero.

items.label: Direction over recorded range
items.description: For a quadratic fit, the unrounded coefficients determine whether the fitted response increases, decreases, stays constant or turns between the lowest and highest recorded concentrations. A stationary endpoint indicates zero slope at that endpoint.

sections.title: Standard points
paragraphs: The record stores 1 to 50 points. The range is an application limit. A successful worksheet fit adds predicted responses and residuals beside the recorded observations. Average calibration factor also shows the factor for each point.

A successful fit adds columns for back-calculated concentration and absolute percent error for each original row, including replicates. When either value is unavailable, the table gives the reason. Before a successful fit, the table shows the recorded points.

items.label: Standard
items.description: The supplied standard/source identifier for each point, in entered order.

items.label: Concentration
items.description: Exact supplied decimal text in the frozen concentration unit, including significant trailing zeros. Concentrations cannot be negative.

items.label: Observed response
items.description: Exact supplied decimal text in the frozen response unit. Signed negative responses are allowed.

items.label: Calibration factor
items.description: For average calibration factor, the observed response divided by concentration for the point. The table shows it in response units per concentration unit.

items.label: Predicted response
items.description: Response calculated from the chosen fit at the recorded concentration, in the frozen response unit.

items.label: Residual
items.description: Observed response minus predicted response, in the frozen response unit. A positive value means the observation is above the prediction. A negative value means it is below.

items.label: Back-calculated concentration
items.description: Use the observed response to solve for concentration in the frozen concentration unit. For Linear, subtract the fitted intercept and divide by the slope. For Linear through origin, divide by the slope directly. For Average calibration factor, divide by the mean factor. A negative slope or mean factor can be used, and the calculated concentration can be negative. A zero slope or mean factor leaves the value unavailable for these models. For Quadratic, the response must increase or decrease in a single direction across the recorded concentration range. A stationary endpoint is allowed. Each observed response must lie between or exactly on the fitted responses at the lowest and highest recorded concentrations. This range also applies when the quadratic coefficient is zero and the fitted response is a straight line.

items.label: Absolute percent error
items.description: The absolute difference between the unrounded back-calculated concentration and the recorded concentration, divided by the recorded concentration and multiplied by 100. A zero recorded concentration or an unavailable back-calculated concentration leaves this value unavailable. Predicted responses and residuals remain visible.

items.label: Maximum error (%)
items.description: The general maximum or the override that applies to this point. This column appears after a successful calculation with a general maximum.

items.label: Limit comparison
items.description: At or below limit includes exact equality. Over limit means the absolute percent error exceeds the applicable maximum. The comparison uses the error before display rounding. If the percent error is unavailable, the worksheet shows Cannot compare.

items.label: Sample
items.description: Lab ID opens the complete result revision history, including the linked revision.

items.label: Analyte
items.description: Frozen analyte on the result revision.

items.label: Revision / Status
items.description: The exact result revision number and workflow state. Earlier revisions remain listed after corrections.

items.label: Calibration verification
items.description: Frozen selected QC label and observation ID, or Not linked. A link never bypasses configured batch QC gates.

items.label: Rows per page / Page links
items.description: Newest entries first. Choose 25, 50 or 100 rows; First, Previous, Next and Last navigate the complete related history. No linked result revisions means no result has explicitly selected this record.

sections.title: History and corrections
paragraphs: The final history panel identifies who recorded the calibration and when. No edit or delete action is available. To correct the evidence, create another calibration reference and then a new result revision with the intended links and reason. Earlier observations, snapshots and issued PDFs remain unchanged.
